nameStory: The zebra mussel gets its name from the dark zigzag stripes that often decorate its shell, resembling the bold patterns of a zebra. However, don't expect every zebra mussel to look like its namesake - some individuals have very faint stripes or none at all, making the name a bit misleading!
description: The zebra mussel is a small freshwater mollusk with a hard, two-part shell that originally came from lakes in southwestern Russia and southeastern Europe. These tiny invaders are usually about the size of your fingernail, though they can grow up to 2 inches long. Their shells have a distinctive D-shape when viewed from the side, and they attach themselves firmly to underwater surfaces using strong, thread-like fibers. Though they may look harmless, these small mussels have become one of the world's most problematic invasive species in freshwater systems.

idTips.label: D-shaped shell
idTips.description: The shell has a triangular or D-shaped profile when viewed from the side, with a straight edge where it attaches to surfaces and a rounded outer edge

idTips.label: Striped pattern
idTips.description: Look for dark brown or black zigzag stripes running across a lighter background, though some individuals may have very faint markings or be solid-colored

idTips.label: Strong attachment
idTips.description: Feel how firmly they're glued to rocks, docks, or other surfaces - they're extremely difficult to remove and attached by tough, rope-like threads

idTips.label: Fingernail size
idTips.description: Most are about the size of your thumbnail or smaller, with a hard shell that feels smooth to the touch when wet

idTips.label: Clustered colonies
idTips.description: Often found in dense clusters covering surfaces, creating a bumpy, crusty texture underwater that you can feel with your hands

idTips.label: Sharp edges
idTips.description: Handle carefully - the shell edges can be quite sharp and will easily cut skin when you're feeling around underwater surfaces

habitat: Zebra mussels live in freshwater lakes, ponds, rivers, and reservoirs throughout New England, particularly in larger water bodies connected to shipping routes. They attach to any hard surface they can find underwater - rocks, boat hulls, dock pilings, water intake pipes, and even other mussels. You'll often find them in areas with moderate water flow and good water quality, though they're adaptable to various freshwater conditions.

seasonality.spring: Adults become more active as water warms, and you'll start to see fresh growth on their shells. This is when they begin their reproductive cycle.
seasonality.summer: Peak reproduction season when microscopic larvae are released into the water. Adult colonies are most visible and easiest to spot on underwater surfaces.
seasonality.fall: Adults continue growing and may produce another generation of offspring before winter. Colonies remain clearly visible on hard surfaces.
seasonality.winter: Adults remain attached to surfaces but become less active in cold water. Ice-free areas still show visible colonies on rocks and structures.

funFact: A single zebra mussel can filter up to one liter of water per day, which sounds helpful until you realize that massive colonies can filter so much water they actually starve out the tiny creatures that native fish depend on for food - essentially eating entire lake ecosystems out of house and home!
confusionNotes: Zebra mussels are sometimes confused with native freshwater mussels, but native mussels are much larger, rounder, and don't attach firmly to hard surfaces - they burrow in sand and mud instead. Remember: if it's small, D-shaped, and super-glued to a rock, it's probably a zebra mussel.
contextualKnowledge: Despite their small size, zebra mussels cause millions of dollars in damage each year by clogging water intake pipes for power plants and water treatment facilities. They arrived in North America accidentally in the 1980s, likely in the ballast water of ships from Europe, and have since spread rapidly through connected waterways.
compareHints: Zebra mussels are closely related to quagga mussels, but quagga mussels have a more rounded shell shape and can survive in deeper, colder water. Quaggas also tend to have less distinct striping and a more fan-shaped shell, while zebra mussels maintain that characteristic D-shape. Both species often live in the same waters, but zebra mussels are more commonly found in shallower areas where recreational boaters are likely to encounter them.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Quagga mussels differ from their close relative, the zebra mussel, primarily in their stripe pattern and shell shape.
